p.x:
Last month, my family moved out of our old apartment and into a new home. The old apartment was small: it had only one bedroom and one bathroom, so my sister and I shared a room with my parents!
Our new home is a small house. It has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a little garden. The owner is a friendly old man who moved to Chiang Mai to live with his daughter.
When we moved in, we were very tired, but very happy. Now we have to pay the bills every month for water and electricity, but my parents say it's worth it. I love having my own room!

Looking for a place to live in Bangkok can be exciting but stressful. Many young workers rent a studio or a small condo near a BTS or MRT station, because the location is very important when traffic is so bad.
First, decide your budget. Remember that rent often doesn't include utilities like water and electricity. Some people share a bigger flat with a flatmate to save money.
Next, contact an estate agent or look online. Arrange a viewing to see the flat before you decide. Check the size (in square metres), whether it's furnished, and how long it has been vacant. Ask the landlord or landlady about the rules for pets and visitors.
If you like it, you'll sign a lease, usually for six or twelve months, and pay a deposit. Read it carefully: if you break the rules, you could face eviction.
Many renters dream of becoming homeowners. However, for a first-time buyer, saving for a down payment is difficult, and interest rates on loans can be high. For many people, housing in the city centre is simply unaffordable. Developers are building new condos everywhere, but construction cannot keep up with demand, so affordability remains a serious problem.

In cities around the world, from London to Bangkok, housing has become a source of anxiety. Prices have soared far faster than wages, and many young people fear they will never own a home. This housing crisis has several causes.
The most basic is supply and demand. As populations grow and people move to cities, demand for homes rises. Supply, however, is limited by land, by zoning rules that restrict what can be built where, and by the time needed to obtain planning permission. When too few homes are built, prices rise.
Financial factors also play a role. Low interest rates make borrowing cheaper, encouraging buyers to pay more. Property speculation, in which investors buy homes not to live in but to sell later at a profit, can push prices up further, and in some cities thousands of apartments stand empty. When prices rise far beyond their real value, economists warn of a bubble. If it bursts and prices plummet, homeowners can be left in negative equity, owing more than their homes are worth. In the worst cases, banks may repossess the properties of borrowers who cannot pay.
Governments have tried many solutions, including building social housing for low-income families, offering grants to first-time buyers, taxing empty homes and introducing rent control to protect tenants. Each approach has critics: some economists argue that rent control reduces the incentive to build. There is no single answer, but most experts agree that the long-term solution must involve building more homes.
